extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating when an invention that consists of the application of a principle or natural truth is a patentable subject — focusing on novelty of the application, required disclosure of a mode of application, enablement, claim scope, and consequences of prior art or disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of the practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle itself must be new in respect to practical application; the principle abstracted from practical application is not within the field of invention. Novelty in the application is essential for a patent that claims the application of a principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the supposed invention is merely the discovery of a law, truth, or force in nature without a new practical application, it is not patentable; the novelty must be in the application to practical uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must invent and describe some mode of carrying the principle into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must have invented and described some mode of carrying the principle into effect; he may or may not have invented new devices, but must show a practical means of effecting the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that simply states a principle without pointing out a mode of conducting the process will be treated as a mere principle and the patent will be invalid. Practitioners should avoid separating the principle from the means of applying it in the specification and claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — description sufficient for skilled persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The means described by the patentee must be so described as to enable competent persons skilled in the art to effect a practical application of the principle (i.e., to work or practise the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether the specification affords enough detail that a workman of competent skill can construct and operate the invention; lack of sufficient description/working examples can render the patent invalid (see Neilson/Bovil evidentiary discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are overly general or claim a principle in the abstract are invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim framed generally for doing something 'by any method' or claiming an art/principle in the abstract is too large and general and cannot be supported as a specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims 'for making gas direct from seeds' without method were held too general; claiming an 'art' (e.g., cutting ice by any non-human power) in the abstract is improper and void unless limited to particular machines or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper claim scope should embrace described means and equivalents performing the same function
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid claim to an application of a principle should be so stated as to embrace directly or by implication the particular means described for the application and all other means which will substantially perform the like office in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may treat later-invented contrivances that substantially perform the same function as equivalent or substituted means (Neilson's hot-blast pipes were treated as equivalent). But claim scope depends on whole specification and surrounding facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art or previous patents can anticipate and defeat a general claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If earlier patents or prior public practice disclose the same general principle or application, a later general claim will be anticipated and cannot be sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a previously-issued patent describing the same general principle defeats a subsequent claim that claims the principle generally; plaintiff may still obtain a patent for a particular method that was novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers can narrow claims and limit the patent's scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may file a disclaimer that limits the original broad claim to a particular described mode, thereby avoiding invalidity for overbreadth but reducing the reach of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will enforce the patent as so limited; a disclaimer may prevent assertion that the patent covers all modes of applying the principle, but also precludes asserting broader coverage against defendants (see Seed v. Higgins and later appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application may be patentable even if the devices used are old
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee need not have invented new devices; giving a practical application of a principle by known means can be the subject of a patent if the application itself is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The means may be new in relation to the application even if old in other contexts; novelty lies in the relation of the means to the application of the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: A technical claim that appears too general may be saved by construing it with the whole specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a technical claim is apparently open to criticism as too general or abstract, it may be saved by a construction that fairly gathers the patentee's intention from the whole specification (i.e., limiting impliedly to the means shown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider the specification as a whole to determine whether the patentee intended to claim the principle abstractly or only its application by the described means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor cannot validly claim all possible future modes of applying the principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee cannot claim a title to all possible or practicable modes of applying a principle or to all future contrivances that may be invented by others; such an attempt would render the claim void as an attempt to monopolize an abstract principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims attempting to appropriate every possible mode (regardless of form) are rejected; proper practice is to claim the described mode and, where appropriate, equivalents that perform the same office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-of-principle plus mechanical contrivances may be treated as part of the invention (basis for infringement vs improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new application of a principle by mechanical contrivances can be regarded as part of the invention itself, and subsequent different or improved modes of application may, in some views, be considered improvements that could still infringe without the patentee's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine is suggested in Foote v. Silsby: variation of the means, even if an improvement, might be treated as an infringement if it performs the same application of the principle, but courts’ application varies with claim language, prior art, and disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims framed as an 'art' or 'principle' rather than a machine or specific method are suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that purport to claim an 'art' or general principle (for example, 'the art of cutting ice by non-human power') instead of a particular machine or method are improper and usually cannot form the basis of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such language is often surplusage or fatal; the proper subject for a patent is a machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a specific practical process, not an abstract 'art' without operative limiting detail.
